knowledge_type_note: A record about a class whose defining property is that class-level principles do not apply to it.

history.notes: Not a tradition with an origin; a residual category in the endgame literature.

engine_era_note: The class most transformed by tablebases, because the hardest mixed endings are small enough to solve and were previously matters of opinion. Several long-held evaluations of specific material balances have been overturned outright.

preconditions: The two sides hold different kinds of material
indicators_for: A passed pawn one side's material is suited to stopping
Pieces that defend one another against a piece that must work alone
recognition.detector: material in lib/features.js reports the counts; the imbalance is visible from them
false_positive_traps: The point count is least reliable exactly here, and this is where people rely on it most. This base holds a proven draw a bishop and a pawn up.
The 60% figure for bishops over knights in endings is a population statistic and says nothing about a particular position.
This class is under-researched in this base, and confidence should stay low regardless of how clean the material description looks.

typical_plans: Ask which side's material suits the pawn structure
Keep two minor pieces defending each other rather than operating separately
Use a knight to blockade a passer and a rook to chase one
Look for a fortress when material down
typical_pawn_structures: Pawns on both wings, which favours the bishop
A symmetrical structure on one wing, which favours the knight
strategic_consequences: Conversion is unusually hard, and fortresses are unusually common

exceptions: Fortresses defeat material reasoning entirely and are common in this class.
The bishop's statistical edge reverses when the pawns are all on one wing.
limitations: This base has not researched mixed-material endings in depth; the record is orientation and says so.
No tablebase-verified position of this class is held here beyond the wrong-rook-pawn and opposite-bishop cases already recorded.
misconceptions: That the point count settles unbalanced endings. It is least reliable precisely here.
That two minor pieces automatically beat a rook. They do when coordinated and lose when they are not.

by_level.beginner: Endings where each side has different pieces — a rook against two minor pieces, say. Counting points helps least here.
by_level.intermediate: What decides them is whether the pieces work together and whose material suits the pawn structure.
by_level.advanced: Bishops beat knights in about 60% of endings, and the more symmetrical the structure the better for the knight — a statistic, not a rule.
by_level.master: The class most rewritten by tablebases, and the one where principles help least.

by_depth.short: Endings with different material on each side.
by_depth.normal: Endings where the two sides hold different kinds of material. They are defined by not being one of the studied types, and the point count - already a rule of thumb - is least reliable exactly here.
by_depth.deep: The endings that are not a type. What decides them is coordination rather than count, since two minor pieces beat a rook when they work together and lose to it when they do not; which side's material suits the pawn structure, since a knight blockades superbly and chases badly while a rook does the reverse; and the presence of fortresses, which live in unbalanced material because a fortress is precisely a position where extra material cannot be converted. The commonest case has a real result behind it - bishops outperform knights in about 60% of endings, and symmetry favours the knight - but that is a statistic about a population and not a claim about any position.

explanations.hedge: Under-researched in this base and orientation rather than theory; where a position is small enough for a tablebase, the tablebase is the authority.
explanations.lesson: Ask whose pieces suit the pawns, not whose pieces add up to more.

definition_short: Endings where the two sides hold different KINDS of material — rook against two minors, queen against rook and pieces, bishop against knight.
definition_long:
The endings that are not a type. Rook-and-pawn endings have a body of theory and named positions; so do knight endings and queen endings. Mixed-material endings are defined by what they are not, and the practical consequence is that the point count — already a rule of thumb — becomes the least reliable guide exactly where people lean on it most.

WHAT ACTUALLY DECIDES THEM:
- COORDINATION over count. Two minor pieces beat a rook when they work together and lose to it when they do not, which is why these endings turn on whether the pieces defend each other and have squares.
- PASSED PAWNS, and specifically who can BLOCKADE. A knight blockades superbly and chases badly; a rook does the opposite. Mixed endings are usually decided by which side's material suits the pawn structure it is facing.
- KING ACTIVITY, as everywhere in the endgame.
- FORTRESSES. Unbalanced material is where fortresses live, because a fortress is precisely a position in which extra material cannot be converted. This base holds proven examples.

THE BISHOP-VERSUS-KNIGHT ENDING is the commonest mixed case and the one with a real result behind it: bishops are better than knights in the endgame roughly 60% of the time, and the more SYMMETRICAL the pawn structure the better for the knight. That is a statistic about a population, not a rule about a position, and this base records it as such.

THE HONEST POSITION on this class is that principles help less here than anywhere else in the endgame, and where a position is small enough for a tablebase the tablebase is the authority. This base has not researched the class in depth and says so.
